summary: Discusses security threats to network-based localized mobility management on two interfaces: between a localized mobility anchor and a mobile access gateway, and between the gateway and a mobile node. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If the network keeps track of moving devices, bad guys might lie to it. This lists the ways attackers could cause trouble at each connection in such a system.

questions: how can attackers compromise localized mobility management
what is the difference between on-link and off-link impersonation
how does denial of service attack netlmm
subtitle: Security risks to network-based mobility management systems that allow devices to move while keeping their IP address.

tldr.problem: Network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM) allows mobile devices to maintain their IP address as they move between access points. This creates new security threats not present in standard IPv6 networks.
tldr.mechanism: The document identifies threats at two critical interfaces: between the mobility anchor and access gateway (control plane), and between the gateway and mobile device (user plane). It also discusses threats from external attackers.
tldr.outcome: This informational document identifies the threats so that protocol specifications for the two interfaces can include appropriate security measures and mitigation strategies.

today: RFC 4832 is an Informational document that continues to describe security threats to NETLMM. It has not been obsoleted and remains a key reference for understanding the security properties and vulnerabilities of network-based mobility management systems.

sections.title: Network-Based Mobility Management
sections.content:
Network-based localized mobility management (NETLMM) is an architecture that lets mobile nodes move within a domain while keeping the same IP address. A localized mobility anchor (LMA) maintains a route to each mobile node, terminating at the mobile access gateway (MAG) where the device currently connects. When a mobile node moves to a different access link, the MAG updates the route at the LMA; the mobile node never changes its IP address or needs special mobility software.

This architecture has two key interfaces: between the LMA and MAG (where route updates happen), and between the MAG and mobile devices (where the device signals its presence and movement). Security threats at either interface can compromise the entire system.
sections.plainLanguage: A special network system lets your phone keep the same number even when you move between locations. The system has two places where bad guys might try to trick it.

sections.title: Threats to the LMA-to-MAG Interface
sections.content:
The control plane between an LMA and MAG handles route setup and teardown for mobile nodes' traffic. Threats include compromise of the LMA, compromise of a MAG, or man-in-the-middle attacks.

A compromised LMA can ignore route updates, create incorrect routes to redirect traffic, or intercept and modify data plane traffic for any mobile node. Since all mobile node traffic flows through the LMA, it is a high-value target. An attacker can also impersonate the LMA, causing a MAG to perform route updates with the attacker instead.

A compromised MAG can redirect a mobile node's traffic without authorization, ignore the mobile node entirely, or trick the LMA into establishing routes for non-existent mobile nodes. This last attack can cause a denial-of-service by forcing the LMA's routing table to grow until it rejects legitimate updates.

An attacker positioned between the LMA and MAG can forge, modify, or drop control plane packets, or impersonate either endpoint. The specific data plane impact depends on whether the attacker is on the data path and what encapsulation mechanism is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might take over the main server or the gateway, or stand in the middle and trick both sides. They could reroute all the traffic going to and from a mobile device.

sections.title: Threats to the MAG-to-Mobile-Node Interface
sections.content:
The second critical interface is where a mobile node connects to a MAG. The MAG must securely bind the mobile node's identity to the link-layer or IP-layer signaling it uses to detect handoffs.

An attacker can forge the mobile node identity to trick a MAG into redirecting traffic to the attacker. On-link attacks do not require route update signaling to the LMA, while off-link attacks require forged handoff signaling. The mobile node can sometimes recover by signaling again on a different handoff, but standard mobile nodes may not detect this kind of attack quickly enough.

Cellular technologies with link-layer authentication make impersonation attacks difficult, but non-cellular access technologies without mandatory authentication are vulnerable. An attacker can also forge handoff signaling to cause denial-of-service by making a MAG think many fictitious mobile nodes have attached, again causing the LMA's routing table to overflow.

IP spoofing is a related threat. While standard network ingress filtering helps, localized mobility management prefixes are not tied to specific links, so topological correctness of IP source addresses is not sufficient; additional address ownership verification is needed.

A man-in-the-middle attack between the mobile node and MAG can allow an attacker to intercept and modify the mobile node's traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might pretend to be a mobile device so the gateway sends them the device's traffic instead. They could also pretend many fake devices are connecting to overload the system.

sections.title: Threats from the Internet
sections.content:
Denial-of-service attacks from outside the localized mobility management domain can target the LMA by sending packets to random IP addresses that might belong to mobile nodes. The LMA must perform routing table lookups on each packet, consuming processing power. For packets with destination addresses not in the routing table, the LMA can drop them early; for others, the LMA must encapsulate and forward them, consuming additional resources.

An attacker can also target a specific globally routable IP address of the LMA or other network entity if that address is known. However, localized mobility management offers some resistance to this attack: mobile nodes never need to know the global IP addresses of LMA or MAG entities, so a compromised mobile node cannot leak this information to external attackers. The large IPv6 address space also makes address scanning slow and impractical.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers from outside can flood the main server with fake messages to random addresses inside the domain. The system can usually handle this better than an IPv6 network because it doesn't have to advertise the addresses of the important machines.
